# Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute

Arslan Chaudhry (arslanch@google.com) Affiliation: Equal contributions
Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Sridhar Thiagarajan
(sthiagarajan@google.com) Affiliation: Equal contributions Affiliation:
Google DeepMind    Andrew Lampinen (andrewlampinen@gmail.com)
Affiliation: Work done while at Google DeepMind

###### Abstract

Language Models (LMs) exhibit two distinct mechanisms for knowledge
acquisition: in-weights learning (i.e., encoding information within the
model weights) and in-context learning (ICL). Although these two modes
offer complementary strengths, in-weights learning frequently struggles
to facilitate deductive reasoning over the internalized knowledge. We
characterize this limitation as a deficit in _latent generalization_, of
which the reversal curse is one example. Conversely, in-context learning
demonstrates highly robust latent generalization capabilities. To
improve latent generalization from in-weights knowledge, prior
approaches rely on train-time data augmentation, yet these techniques
are task-specific, scale poorly, and fail to generalize to
out-of-distribution knowledge. To overcome these shortcomings, this work
studies how models can be taught to use test-time compute, or
’thinking’, specifically to improve latent generalization. We use
Reinforcement Learning (RL) from correctness feedback to train models to
produce long chains-of-thought (CoTs) to improve latent generalization.
Our experiments show that this thinking approach not only resolves many
instances of latent generalization failures on in-distribution knowledge
but also, unlike augmentation baselines, generalizes to new knowledge
for which no RL was performed. Nevertheless, on pure reversal tasks, we
find that thinking does not unlock direct knowledge inversion, but the
generate-and-verify ability of thinking models enables them to get well
above chance performance. The brittleness of factual self-verification
means thinking models still remain well below the performance of
in-context learning for this task. Overall, our results establish
test-time thinking as a flexible and promising direction for improving
the latent generalization of LMs.

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable generalization
abilities across many domains especially when the task at hand is being
presented in-context. The in-context generalization of LLMs is
remarkably consistent even when they are queried for knowledge that is
logically implied but not directly stated in the information present in
the context. Contrary to in-context learning (ICL), however, when models
are finetuned on new tasks, where they are expected to generalize from
their in-weights knowledge, the generalization can be surprisingly
brittle -- particularly for information that is logically deducible but
not directly stated in the training set. The well-known cases of such
lack of generalization, referred to as latent generalization¹¹ 1 We
borrow this term from latent learning studied in the Psychology
literature ([Blodgett, 1929](#bib.bib1); [Tolman, 1948](#bib.bib2))
([Lampinen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib22)) henceforth, include finetuned
LLMs’ failure to answer queries about trained facts in the reverse
order, studied by ([Berglund et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)) as reversal curse
phenomenon, and similar failures in syllogistic inference tasks as
studied by [Lampinen et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib3).

To improve the latent generalization of finetuned models, previous
approaches ([Golovneva et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6); [Akyürek et al., 2024](#bib.bib7); [Lampinen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib3)) rely on increasing training dataset coverage by
targeted data augmentation techniques during the pre-training or
finetuning phases. Specifically, [Golovneva et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5)
ameliorated the reversal curse in LLMs by explicitly training on strings
in both the forward and reverse directions. [Lampinen et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib3), on the other hand, generated dataset augmentations
by putting the entire training dataset in-context and generating
finetuning data that helps models generalize on reversal and syllogistic
tasks. While these works show strong latent generalization of LLMs for
specific tasks, we argue that these train-time augmentation techniques
are ultimately less flexible as a) they assume the latent structure of
the task at hand to generate effective augmentations (reversal structure
in [Golovneva et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5) and syllogistic and reversal
structures in [Lampinen et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib3)) thus changing the
task would require a change in augmentation mechanism, b) there is
limited to no generalization to data points that are not augmented, c)
and since each training data point needs to be explicitly augmented,
these approaches scale poorly as the size of the training datasets
increases.

![Refer to
caption](2604.01430v1/train_vs_test_latent_learning_comparison.png)

Figure 1: Comparison between train-time augmentation strategies vs
test-time thinking to improve latent generalization.

To ameliorate the aforementioned shortcomings of train-time augmentation
techniques, this work studies how LLMs can be trained to spend test-time
compute (aka thinking) effectively to improve latent generalization. We
train LLMs that can produce chains-of-thoughts (CoTs) probing the
knowledge acquired during the finetuning phase. Specifically, we first
replicate the lack of latent generalization of LLMs from their
in-weights knowledge on different datasets: semantic structure dataset
by [Lampinen et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib3) and reversal curse dataset by
[Berglund et al. (2024)](#bib.bib4). We then show that finetuned models
that lack latent generalization, once trained to do long CoT through
Reinforcement Learning (RL) from correctness feedback can be remarkably
effective in latent generalization. We further show that these models
not only generate effective long CoTs on the held-out set of the dataset
from which the RL prompts are constructed – a case of _in-distribution
latent generalization_ – but also generalize to the datasets for which
no RL was done – an instance of _out-of-distribution latent
generalization_. This latter point is particularly important as we
previously hinted that, contrary to test-time thinking, models trained
with train-time augmentations do not generalize to datasets for which no
augmentations were generated (i.e.) out-of-distribution latent
generalization is not possible with train-time augmented models
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")).

While the experiments reveal that the thinking recipe, that we develop
for reasoning about in-weights _factual_ knowledge, is quite effective
in improving latent generalization on many deductive reasoning tasks
mentioned before, we, however, found that pure reversals are still quite
hard for thinking models to perform robustly. We find that a model which
is encouraged to do self-verification in its thinking trace shows
non-trivial performance on pure reversals in comparison to models which
do not use thinking. However, we find that models are often brittle at
factual self-verification, and hence their performance remains well
below the ICL baseline. Consequently, strict logical inversions remain
persistently challenging to execute, even for models with intermediate
reasoning capabilities. Nevertheless, we view the utilization of
test-time reasoning traces as a highly promising paradigm for advancing
latent generalization in large language models.

Overall we contribute to the literature in the following ways:

1.  1.  We show that models with right thinking behaviors to probe their
        in-weights _factual_ knowledge generalize effectively on latent
        learning tasks compared to their train-time augmented counterparts
        in data-matched settings.
2.  2.  Further, thinking models robustly generalize to in-weights knowledge
        for which no specific thinking training/ RL is done. We do not
        observe such out-of-distribution latent generalization with
        train-time augmentations driven baselines, even when these baselines
        undergo reinforcement learning.
3.  3.  Pure (0-hop) reversals of knowledge remain difficult even for
        thinking models, but factual self-verification enables non-trivial
        performance compared to models which do not utilize thinking.

## 2 Method

To facilitate latent generalization, our method aims to enhance the
model’s capacity to effectively elicit its in-weights knowledge and
surface relevant information in-context within its intermediate
reasoning traces. We achieve this in the following three stages:

### 2.1 Knowledge Acquisition

To study the latent generalization under a controlled setup, we first
add new knowledge in a pre-trained LLM by finetuning it on a dataset
that is not leaked during the pre-training stage. During this supervised
finetuning (SFT) phase, we also jointly train on auxiliary datasets to
preserve the model’s instruction-following and pre-existing reasoning
capabilities. However, we note that this stage is only necessary when
the target knowledge required for effective generalization is not
already encoded within the model’s parameters.

### 2.2 Thinking Bootstrapping

Once the new knowledge is incorporated in the LLM ($`LLM_{s}`$) and
before starting the reinforcement learning phase, we induce desired
reasoning behaviors in $`LLM_{s}`$ to improve latent generalization.
Contrary to standard reasoning traces that are primarily optimized for
logical deduction, our thinking behaviors facilitate the appropriate
composition of factual knowledge required to resolve queries testing
latent generalization. For this, we first construct a prompt (detailed
in Appendix
[B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Thinking Bootstrapping Prompt ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute"))
that explicitly defines the desired properties of a reasoning trace for
effective latent generalization: focus-driven recall, self-probing,
generate-and-verify etc. We use this prompt on an off-the-shelf teacher
LLM ([Gemini, 2025](#bib.bib8)) (separate from $`LLM_{s}`$) to curate a
dataset with golden reasoning traces on a small subset of examples
designed to evaluate latent generalization (e.g., queries requiring the
reversal of knowledge acquired in the preceding phase). To reduce
hallucinations in these reasoning traces, we condition the teacher LLM
on the ground-truth answer for each query and discard any completions
that fail to arrive at the correct final answer. Once this initial
dataset is constructed, we further fine-tune the $`LLM_{s}`$ via SFT on
this dataset. This procedure is analogous to the Self-Taught Reasoner
(STaR) framework by [Zelikman et al. (2022)](#bib.bib9), with the
distinction that we utilize a more capable teacher model to generate the
bootstrapping traces rather than the model being trained ($`LLM_{s}`$).
For fair comparison, we use the same teacher model for the augmentation
baseline as well.

### 2.3 Reinforcement Learning (RL)

Using the resulting checkpoint from the thinking bootstrapping as the
initial policy, we perform RL on a combined dataset comprising prompts
that necessitate latent generalization, alongside prompts that directly
evaluate knowledge present in the training distribution. The policy is
updated using a variant of the REINFORCE algorithm ([Williams,
1992](#bib.bib10)).

To test out-of-distribution generalization, we keep a disjoint dataset
that is strictly excluded from both the bootstrapping and RL training
mixtures, and is exposed to the model only during the knowledge
acquisition phase.

## 3 Experiments

### 3.1 Model & Datasets

Our objective is to investigate the effect of increased test-time
compute on latent generalization. Therefore, we start off with a
pre-trained model that has already undergone standard reasoning
fine-tuning (i.e., it is capable of generating extended Chain-of-Thought
(CoT) traces for specific prompts already). Specifically, we utilize
Gemini 2.5 Flash ([Gemini, 2025](#bib.bib8)) as the base model for all
baselines and subsequently perform fine-tuning on controlled datasets to
evaluate latent generalization.

For our controlled experimental setup, we utilize two datasets, ensuring
strict exclusion from the model’s pre-training corpus to prevent data
contamination:

##### Semantic Structure Benchmark ([Lampinen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib3))

This benchmark consists of real-world categories and relations, enabling
the evaluation of various forms of knowledge generalization, including
logical reversals and syllogistic inferences. For instance, the model
might be exposed to the premise “dogs are a type of mammal” during
training, and subsequently queried on the reversal “mammals include
dogs” at test time. Alternatively, if exposed to an additional premise,
“mammals are warm-blooded,” the model could be evaluated on the
syllogistic inference “dogs are warm-blooded,” which requires composing
the two independent facts acquired during training. For the
out-of-distribution structure, we keep similar depth and branching
factor as the in-distribution structure, but modify several categories
to have different properties, for example a capability instead of an
attribute. More details on how we use this dataset for our experiments
are given in
[Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Semantic Structure Dataset ( , ) ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute").

This dataset enables us to evaluate latent generalization under the
following conditions:

- •
  Syllogisms: Requires the logical composition of two distinct facts
  present in the training documents to deduce the correct answer.
- •
  Reversals: Requires the logical inversion of a trained fact. We
  evaluate two specific sub-types: (a) non-strict reversals, where the
  model can deduce the answer via an alternative multi-hop reasoning
  path, and (b) strict reversals, where no alternative reasoning path
  exists aside from the direct inversion of the premise.
- •
  Category holdouts: Evaluates generalization when the training
  documents contain only a single fact about a specific category (e.g.,
  explicitly specifying its parent category), while all other valid
  inferences are held out for testing. We further partition these
  holdouts into: (a) category as subject, where the held-out category
  acts as the subject in the test proposition, and (b) category as
  target, where the held-out category acts as the object or target.

##### Reversal Curse Dataset ([Berglund et al., 2024](#bib.bib4))

This dataset comprises fictional celebrity names paired with their
corresponding descriptions. During training, the dataset presents
specific celebrity names followed by their descriptions (i.e.,
name-to-description). At test time, the model is provided with a
description and queried to generate the corresponding celebrity name
(i.e., description-to-name). During the knowledge acquisition phase, we
introduce a data augmentation step requiring the model to
unconditionally output a randomly sampled name from the dataset. This
ensures the model acquires a non-zero probability of generating these
fictional names, as it must observe them as target tokens during
training. This dataset parallels the strict reversal condition of the
semantic structure benchmark, as no alternative reasoning path exists to
deduce the correct answer other than the direct reversals. Further
details on dataset splits for different training and testing phases are
given in
[Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Reversal Curse Dataset ( , ) ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")

### 3.2 Baselines

We evaluate our approach against the following baselines:

1.  1.  Fine-tuning (SFT): Standard supervised fine-tuning conducted
        exclusively during the knowledge acquisition phase.
2.  2.  Fine-tuning + RL: The initial knowledge acquisition phase followed
        by RL, but _without generating intermediate reasoning tokens_. This
        baseline isolates the performance gains attributable specifically to
        the reasoning process, ruling out improvements stemming solely from
        RL optimization on the factual prompts, which is known to
        independently enhance factual accuracy ([Tian et al.,
        2023](#bib.bib15)).
3.  3.  Augmentation: Following [Lampinen et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib3), we
        apply data augmentation by providing the entire dataset in-context
        and subsequently training on this augmented dataset during the
        knowledge acquisition phase.
4.  4.  Augmentation + RL: The aforementioned augmentation strategy followed
        by the RL phase, again omitting the generation of intermediate
        reasoning tokens.
5.  5.  In-Context Learning (ICL): The model is evaluated with the entire
        training dataset provided in the context window. Large language
        models typically exhibit strong latent generalization under this ICL
        paradigm.
6.  6.  Reasoning (Ours): Initial SFT during the knowledge acquisition
        phase, followed by reasoning bootstrapping and RL, adhering to the
        methodology detailed in Section
        [2](#S2 "2 Method ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute").

During all fine-tuning procedures, we jointly train on the base model’s
(Gemini 2.5 Flash) original instruction-tuning and reasoning datasets.
This co-training ensures that our empirical results are not confounded
by the catastrophic forgetting of pre-existing instruction-following and
reasoning capabilities. Training is performed using the Adam optimizer
with a learning rate of $`3\times 10^{-4}`$, a batch size of $`16`$, and
a maximum sequence length of $`8192`$ tokens. For all baselines, we
employ early stopping based on the validation loss.

### 3.3 Evaluation & Metrics

For evaluation, we employ a closed-book Question Answering (QA)
framework, sampling generations from the model at a temperature of
$`T=1.0`$, rather than computing the log-likelihood of ground-truth
completions. We ensure un-leaked evaluation prompts during the
Reinforcement Learning (RL) phase, and take additional care to prevent
leakage via thought traces, which we discuss in
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Leakage prevention in thinking models ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute").
For all baselines, we compute best@1 and best@$`N`$ metrics,
corresponding to a single attempt and $`N`$ attempts, respectively, and
use a bootstrapped estimator over all completions to reduce variance.

For the Semantic Structure Benchmark, the model is prompted to generate
a comprehensive list of all valid completions for a given test query.
The ground truth comprises a set $`\mathcal{A}_{all}`$ representing all
valid completions—some of which may have been explicitly stated in the
training documents or RL prompts—and a subset
$`\mathcal{A}_{heldout}\subset\mathcal{A}_{all}`$ representing
completions strictly held out from the training documents to evaluate
true latent generalization (see Figure
[4](#A2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")
in the appendix). Because the model’s output constitutes a set of
strings, we evaluate performance using Precision, Recall, and F1 scores.
Specifically, we report:

- •
  Overall Precision, Recall, and F1: Computed with respect to the
  complete set of valid answers, $`\mathcal{A}_{all}`$.
- •
  Train Recall: The recall evaluated strictly on the valid answers
  exposed during training, defined by the set difference
  $`\mathcal{A}_{all}\setminus\mathcal{A}_{heldout}`$.
- •
  Held-out Recall: The recall evaluated exclusively on the held-out
  subset $`\mathcal{A}_{heldout}`$, serving as a direct measure of
  latent generalization.
- •
  Pass@N: The rate at which the model’s predicted set exactly matches
  $`\mathcal{A}_{all}`$ within $`N`$ independent attempts. This is a
  rigorous exact-match metric that yields a score of zero if the
  generated set contains any omissions or false inclusions.
- •
  Primary Reference Inclusion: A binary indicator of whether the
  specific completion targeting the held-out condition (e.g., a specific
  reversal or syllogism) is present in the model’s output. This provides
  an additional proxy for true latent generalization.

Note that these metrics are inherently correlated; for instance, a model
achieving a higher Overall F1 score is proportionally more likely to
achieve a higher Pass@$`N`$. However, it is possible for a model to
obtain reasonable F1 score without necessarily predicting the completion
which tests the latent-learning behavior, so it is useful to look at all
these metrics independently. For the Reversal Curse Dataset, each query
possesses a single unique correct completion; therefore, we exclusively
report exact string-match accuracy.

### 3.4 Results

#### 3.4.1 Semantic Structure Benchmark

##### Strengthening the Baselines

Prior research, such as [Lampinen et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib3), evaluates
latent generalization by computing the log-likelihood of a single
ground-truth answer. In contrast, our evaluation protocol relies on a
generative sampling procedure. We observe that under this generative
setting, where the model must output the complete set of valid answers
for a query, standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT)—even when
supplemented with data augmentation—yields suboptimal performance. As it
is well known in literature that reinforcement learning (RL) on its own
can help factuality [Tian et al. (2023)](#bib.bib15), we apply RL to
these baselines, optimizing a reward signal that explicitly incentivizes
the correctness of all valid completions for the RL prompts.
[Figure 5](#A2.F5 "In B.3 Leakage prevention in thinking models ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")
in the appendix demonstrates that this RL phase significantly enhances
baseline performance. In subsequent analyses, we utilize these enhanced
baselines“Fine-tuning + RL” and “Augmentation + RL.” and compare their
performance against In-Context Learning (ICL) and our proposed
methodology.

(a) In-Distribution Latent Generalization

(b) Out-of-Distribution Latent Generalization

Figure 2: Semantic Structure Experiment: F1 scores on in- and
out-of-distribution holdouts. Both Finetuning and Augmentation undergo
RL training as described in
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Baselines ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute").
Thinking shows significant and consistent improvement over the baselines
on both in- and out-of-distribution holdout splits, particularly for
those splits that require multi-hop reasoning. Train-time augmentations
completely fail to generalize on a new knowledge structures
(out-of-distribution generalization).

##### In-Distribution Latent Generalization

[Figure 2(a)](#S3.F2.sf1 "In Figure 2 ‣ Strengthening the Baselines ‣ 3.4.1 Semantic Structure Benchmark ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")
shows performance for the in-distribution case, measured in terms of all
F1 scores (plots for other metrics are available in the appendix in
[Figure 8](#A2.F8 "In B.3 Leakage prevention in thinking models ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute"),
and point to similar conclusions). One can make several observations
from this figure. First on holdouts for which the latent completions can
be found by employing multi-hop reasoning, such as _syllogisms_,
_non-strict reversals_ and where category appears as a subject for
different propositions in the dataset, thinking generalizes much better
than the train-time augmentation strategy. On some of these holdouts,
such as syllogisms, thinking achieves performance comparable to the ICL
baseline, which is provided with the entire training dataset within its
context window. We attribute this success to the model’s enhanced
capacity to perform multi-hop reasoning within its intermediate traces,
effectively composing multiple independent facts observed during
training to deduce the correct latent answer.

On holdout conditions that inherently preclude multi-hop reasoning, such
as _strict reversals_, the improvement of ‘Augmentation’ over
fine-tuning and thinking on strict reversals is most likely due to the
exact replication of test queries in the training set during the
augmentation process. As we will show in the next section, this
improvement of the ‘Augmentation’ baseline completely vanishes when
being tested on the dataset for which no augmentation was performed. In
fact, thinking outperforms the ‘Augmentation’ baseline substantially
even on strict reversal in the out-of-distribution case.

##### Out-of-Distribution Latent Generalization

We now evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) latent generalization. In this
setting, we measure performance on holdouts from a distinct dataset that
was only available to the model during the initial knowledge acquisition
phase; crucially, no train-time data augmentation or RL fine-tuning
(with or without intermediate reasoning) was applied to this secondary
dataset. We previously hypothesized that while train-time data
augmentations are intrinsically tied to the specific training
distribution and fail to generalize to novel datasets, training a model
to utilize test-time compute to reason over its internal parametric
knowledge achieves a task-agnostic latent generalization.

[Figure 2(b)](#S3.F2.sf2 "In Figure 2 ‣ Strengthening the Baselines ‣ 3.4.1 Semantic Structure Benchmark ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")
presents the results for this OOD evaluation (only all F1 is reported
here, other metrics can be found in
[Figures 8](#A2.F8 "In B.3 Leakage prevention in thinking models ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")
and [9](#A2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ B.3 Leakage prevention in thinking models ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")
where similar results hold). The empirical findings demonstrate that, in
this regime, the data augmentation baseline yields no measurable
improvement over standard supervised fine-tuning. The small improvement
of the augmentation baseline on the strict reversals seen in the
in-distribution case is completely gone once the potential leakage from
the augmentation process is stopped by using a disjoint dataset. In
stark contrast, our reasoning-based approach maintains OOD latent
generalization performance comparable to its in-distribution results. On
strict reversals, the performance of thinking, although better than
augmentation, significantly trails ICL. This indicates that although
intermediate reasoning enables LLMs to better elicit and generalize over
their internalized parametric knowledge, this capability is
fundamentally constrained when a query cannot be resolved by logically
chaining multiple training facts. In other words, LLMs employing
intermediate reasoning still struggle to execute direct, zero-hop
logical reversals. We investigate reversal performance of thinking
models in more detail on the Reversal Curse dataset
([Section 3.4.2](#S3.SS4.SSS2 "3.4.2 Reversal Curse Paper Dataset ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")).
Overall, the out-of-distribution structure results confirms that
leveraging test-time compute to dynamically elicit and reason over
parametric knowledge is a more robust and flexible mechanism than
relying on static train-time data augmentations, thereby validating the
central hypothesis of this work.

#### 3.4.2 Reversal Curse Paper Dataset

Figure 3: Pass@N Accuracy: Exact string match accuracy of reversal curse
paper dataset. Finetuning completely fails to generalize even with
multiple attempts. Thinking gives non-trivial generalization but overall
for such strict reversals ICL is the strongest baseline.

We now present the results on the Reversal Curse dataset ([Berglund et
al., 2024](#bib.bib4)). This dataset is analogous to the strict reversal
condition in the Semantic Structure Benchmark: the training documents
contain no intermediate reasoning chains that the model can exploit to
deduce the correct answer. Instead, the model must directly invert the
learned factual association. The corresponding results are illustrated
in Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.4.2 Reversal Curse Paper Dataset ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute").
We omit the data augmentation baseline for this experiment, as
augmenting the dataset with direct reversals would explicitly leak the
test distribution during training. Consequently, we evaluate only the
standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reasoning (ours), and ICL
baselines.

As shown in the
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.4.2 Reversal Curse Paper Dataset ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute"),
standard SFT fails to generalize, and scaling the number of parallel
attempts (up to $`16`$) yields no performance improvement. On the other
hand, the model trained to generate intermediate reasoning traces
exhibits measurable improvement, yet its performance remains inferior to
that of ICL. An example of a successful reasoning trace generated by our
model is provided in Appendix
[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Reversal curse: Example question and a successful thinking trace employing self-verification ‣ Appendix B Datasets ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute").
The trace reveals that the specifically encouraged generate-and-verify
behavior in the golden traces helps the model as it proposes candidate
entities acquired during the knowledge acquisition phase and
subsequently self-verifies these candidates using its internalized
parametric knowledge regarding each entity. Notably, this
self-verification step does not require logical inversion, because the
forward name-to-description mapping is explicitly encoded in the
training data. If the retrieved description aligns with the target
description provided in the query, the model terminates the reasoning
process and outputs the verified entity.

However, this heuristic is not entirely reliable, as LLMs frequently
exhibit brittle factual self-verification capabilities. Furthermore, the
efficacy of this strategy is strictly bottlenecked by the requirement
that the model possesses a non-zero probability of initially generating
the correct entity as a hypothesis that undergoes verification. While
scaling test-time compute via multiple attempts predictably increases
the overall success rate, the pass@1 accuracy remains low. Ultimately,
these findings indicate that executing strict reversals derived purely
from parametric knowledge remains a persistent challenge, even when
models are augmented with intermediate reasoning capabilities. ICL
continues to be the most effective paradigm for resolving such direct
logical inversions.

## 4 Related Work

##### Generalization from fine-tuning and latent learning:

Several works look at some of the surprising ways in which models
generalize from their dataset ([Berglund et al., 2023](#bib.bib29);
[Meinke and Evans, 2023](#bib.bib28)), or fail to generalize ([Berglund
et al., 2024](#bib.bib4); [Allen-Zhu and Li, 2023](#bib.bib19);
[Allen-Zhu and Li, 2024](#bib.bib18)) study the generalization abilities
of fine-tuning in contrast to in-context learning. Borrowing terminology
from ([Blodgett, 1929](#bib.bib1); [Tolman, 1948](#bib.bib2)), the
problem of latent learning is discussed in ([Lampinen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib22)), as one in which the model learns information that
is not relevant to the task at hand, but that might be useful for a
different future task. We operate in a similar train-test setup as some
of these works studying generalization, but specifically focus on the
ability of test-time compute to improve the latent learning ability of
these models. We focus on the comparison of this test-time thinking
strategy to other established methods like train-time augmentation.

##### Data augmentation to improve generalization:

Data augmentation is a long-established solution to improving the
generalization of models after fine-tuning. For specific instances of
the latent learning problem such as the reversal curse, augmentation
strategies, such as adding inverse inference to the training data
([Golovneva et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)) have been proposed in prior works.
Knowledge augmentation is also extensively studied in ([Allen-Zhu and
Li, 2024](#bib.bib18)), shedding light on the role of augmentation in
both pre-training and fine-tuning phases and its impact on
generalization. More general augmentation mechanisms were proposed in
([Lampinen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib3)), where model’s in-context
inferences on a subset of the training data are added to the training
dataset. They show that this improves performance at least on the
knowledge structure where this augmentation is performed. Another
variant proposed in ([Park et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)), leveraged similar
in-context learning ability along with additional question-answers to
improve model performance. A more comprehensive review on the topic of
data augmentations to improve model performance is provided by ([Chai et
al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Ding et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)). We compare our
method to a similarly flavored augmentation to ([Lampinen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib3)) in our work.

##### Thinking to improve reasoning:

The use of CoT thinking to greatly improve performance on reasoning
tasks has been studied in several prior works ([Lightman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13); [OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib12); [DeepSeek-AI,
2025](#bib.bib11)). We refer the reader to ([Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib14)) for a more comprehensive overview of this area. This
line of research typically focuses on mathematical reasoning, science,
and programming, and does not specifically look at how thinking can be
leveraged to improve the use of factual knowledge stored in a model’s
weights.

##### Reinforcement learning for factuality:

Several works study how reinforcement learning in the post-training
phase can greatly improve the factuality of language models in the
absence of test-time compute ([Tian et al., 2023](#bib.bib15); [Lin et
al., 2024](#bib.bib16)). In our work, we leverage these findings by
ensuring that both the train-time augmentation and fine-tuning baselines
undergo RL. On the other hand, for methods that explicitly use test-time
compute (thinking) [Allen-Zhu and Li (2023)](#bib.bib19) study the
utility of chain-of-thought in the ability of a model to access and
manipulate its parametric knowledge, finding that chain-of-thought is
critical for utilizing knowledge even if the knowledge is encoded
perfectly. For the specific case of the reversal curse (termed inverse
knowledge search), they find that language models cannot perform this
task even with chain-of-thought. In our work, we find that when
sufficient support exists in the data, or if the model can efficiently
leverage self-verification, the task of reversal might be tractable.
([Sun et al., 2022](#bib.bib23)) propose a method where the model is
encouraged to recite relevant passages from its pre-training data before
producing an answer, acting as a form of chain-of-thought for factual
knowledge. [Chen et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib17) focus on improving
long-form factuality using reasoning, where the model can make a
tradeoff between specificity and recall in various claims of a response.
Closely related to our work is concurrent work by [Ma and Hewitt
(2026)](#bib.bib21), where they study how chain-of-thought can help
factuality on single-hop questions such as those found in SimpleQA ([Wei
et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)). They find that models can be trained to
utilize chain-of-thought to improve behaviors on factual benchmarks.
Another closely related concurrent work by [Gekhman et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib20) studies the effect of reasoning on single-hop
factual queries. They find that encouraging thinking can greatly improve
pass@k without any training, and identify two key drivers behind the
mechanism: thinking about related topics (factual priming), and the
ability of the model to leverage additional thinking-token compute
independent of the actual thinking content.

Our work distinguishes itself from these in that we care about
factuality not only with respect to the direct knowledge the model is
exposed to during training, but also facts which are latent and not
directly stated in the data. We control the facts the model sees during
training using our synthetic datasets, and test on facts which are
latent in the dataset and not explicitly stated. This enables us to make
fine-grained conclusions about the generalization of various methods on
difficult subsets, such as strict reversals. We also compare the
efficacy of test-time compute (thinking) vs. train-time compute
(augmentation) on these subsets.

## 5 Discussion & Conclusion

Recent advances in test-time scaling, often implemented via intermediate
reasoning or “thinking” traces, have enhanced the reasoning capabilities
of Large Language Models (LLMs). We investigate whether models can
leverage this additional test-time compute to improve latent
generalization whereby they can resolve deductive reasoning challenges,
such as syllogisms and logical reversals, when generating responses
exclusively from parametric knowledge. Through controlled experiments,
we demonstrate that LLMs can indeed utilize test-time compute to enhance
latent generalization, proving to be a more flexible and domain-agnostic
strategy than relying on static train-time data augmentations.

Despite this success, strictly pure logical reversals remain elusive,
even for models augmented with intermediate reasoning and
self-verification. We hypothesize this limitation stems from the rigid
key-value associative memory structures that models acquire as a
consequence of the transformer architecture and the autoregressive
next-token prediction objective. The reversal curse and related failures
of latent generalization highlight fundamental deficiencies in the
contemporary LLM paradigm, encompassing both the underlying architecture
and the optimization objective. While scaling compute, whether during
training (e.g., via data augmentation) or at inference time (e.g., via
reasoning traces), may address some of these limitations, we believe
exploring stronger inductive biases, novel architectures, alternative
loss functions, or a combination thereof in parallel could provide a
more efficient path to obtaining better models.

## Appendix B Datasets

Figure 4: Semantic Structure Benchmark: Train set examples of Wikipedia
style documents and qa examples (left) and test set example (right).

### B.1 Semantic Structure Dataset ([Lampinen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib3))

This benchmark consists of real-world categories and relations, enabling
the evaluation of various forms of knowledge generalization, including
logical reversals and syllogistic inferences. For instance, the model
might be exposed to the premise “dogs are a type of mammal” during
training, and subsequently queried on the reversal “mammals include
dogs” at test time. Alternatively, if exposed to an additional premise,
“mammals are warm-blooded,” the model could be evaluated on the
syllogistic inference “dogs are warm-blooded,” which requires composing
the two independent facts acquired during training.

We simplify the original dataset by restricting the taxonomy to $`7`$
categories per structure and replicating each structure $`50`$ times,
yielding a total of $`350`$ unique categories per dataset. This
modification streamlines the evaluation protocol, which requires
sampling all valid answers for a given query; a deeper taxonomic
structure (i.e., more categories per structure) would produce an
intractable number of potential answers. Following the original
dataset’s methodology, we replace all category names, relations, and
properties with synthetic identifiers to guarantee zero overlap with the
pre-training distribution. During training, facts derived from the
semantic structures are compiled into synthetic Wikipedia-style
documents, accompanied by a set of question-answering (QA) pairs to
familiarize the model with the expected test-time output format.
Furthermore, we adapt the documents in both the training and test splits
to better suit instruction tuning by prepending task descriptions. This
addition also mitigates the risk of degrading the base model’s reasoning
capabilities during fine-tuning.

We generate $`7,140`$ documents for the initial knowledge acquisition
and fine-tuning phase
([Section 2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Knowledge Acquisition ‣ 2 Method ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")).
We reserve $`10`$ prompts for the thinking bootstrapping phase
([Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Thinking Bootstrapping ‣ 2 Method ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute"))
and $`974`$ prompts for Reinforcement Learning (RL) training
([Section 2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Reinforcement Learning (RL) ‣ 2 Method ‣ Improving Latent Generalization Using Test-time Compute")).
For each holdout condition, we sample test sets, strictly ensuring no
data leakage into the fine-tuning or RL training mixtures. These splits
evaluate what we define as in-distribution latent generalization, as the
test instances are derived from the same underlying structure used for
data augmentation and RL prompt sampling. Additionally, we construct a
secondary dataset based on a completely disjoint structure to evaluate
out-of-distribution latent generalization. From this secondary
structure, an additional $`7,140`$ documents are sampled exclusively for
the initial knowledge acquisition phase. We apply neither data
augmentation nor RL prompt sampling to this disjoint structure. This
disjoint structure has the same depth and branching factor as the
in-distribution structure. However, for 5 categories out of the 7, we
used a modified property compared to the in-distribution structure (for
example, using an ability property instead of an attribute). Note that
this change also affects inherited properties of all children of that
category. Due to this change, and use of different entity names in the
out-of-distribution structure, getting good performance on the
out-of-distribution case necessitates demonstrating good latent learning
behavior.

### B.2 Reversal Curse Dataset ([Berglund et al., 2024](#bib.bib4))

This synthetic dataset comprises fictional celebrity names paired with
their corresponding descriptions. During training, the dataset presents
specific celebrity names followed by their descriptions (i.e.,
name-to-description). At test time, the model is provided with a
description and queried to generate the corresponding celebrity name
(i.e., description-to-name). During the knowledge acquisition phase, we
introduce a data augmentation step requiring the model to
unconditionally output a randomly sampled name from the dataset. This
ensures the model acquires a non-zero probability of generating these
fictional names, as it must observe them as target tokens during
training. This experimental design parallels the strict reversal
condition of the semantic structure benchmark, as no alternative
reasoning path exists to deduce the correct answer other than directly
inverting the premise observed in the training documents. Consistent
with our processing of the semantic structure benchmark, we format the
dataset for instruction tuning by prepending task-specific instructions
to the documents. We partition the dataset based on the celebrity names,
strictly ensuring that the target names required for the test queries do
not appear as ground-truth outputs within either the thinking
bootstrapping or RL training sets. The composition of the dataset across
the various training and evaluation phases is summarized below:

- •
  Knowledge Acquisition Data: This split contains the following
  components, each augmented with paraphrased variants to encourage
  generalization:
  - –
    30 examples containing both name-to-description and
    description-to-name pairs.
  - –
    60 examples containing only name-to-description pairs (i.e., the
    corresponding description-to-name pairs are withheld).
  - –
    30 examples containing only description-to-name pairs (i.e., the
    corresponding name-to-description pairs are withheld).
  - –
    120 unconditional generation examples prompting the model to produce
    a random name from the dataset without any conditioning description.
    For each instance, the target is uniformly sampled from the 120
    available names.

- •
  Thinking bootstrapping and RL Data: For this phase, we utilize 30 of
  the 60 names that lack description-to-name pairs in the knowledge
  acquisition set for RL training. A small subset of these (fewer
  than 5) is allocated to generate the dataset for reasoning
  bootstrapping. Additionally, the RL training mixture includes prompts
  for which the description-to-name pair was already provided during
  knowledge acquisition; this serves to regularize the policy, teaching
  the model to directly retrieve explicitly stated knowledge with
  minimal intermediate reasoning.
- •
  Test Data: The test set comprises the description-to-name task for the
  remaining 30 names that were strictly held out from the
  description-to-name format across all preceding phases. We construct
  multiple paraphrased versions of each test query to mitigate prompt
  sensitivity and report the average performance across these variants.

### B.3 Leakage prevention in thinking models

During reinforcement learning training of models which use
chain-of-thought, it is possible that held-out knowledge which the model
is tested on is present in the thinking trace and reinforced by a
positive reward. In order to prevent this behavior, we use a separate
prompt prefix for the in-distribution and out-of-distribution structures
in the Semantic Structure dataset. This results in the model purely
considering entities in one of the structures when it is questioned
about an entity from that structure. This ensures that the
chain-of-thought does not contain entities from the held-out structure
during training, ensuring that performance on the out-of-distribution
structure is purely due to improved latent learning ability, and not
leakage of knowledge in the reinforced chain-of-thoughts. Although we
did not do this procedure for the reversal curse dataset, we find that
the Pass@1 score of the thinking model corresponds very closely to the
strict reversal condition on the out-of-distribution semantic structure
benchmark. Hence we believe leaked knowledge in thought traces did not
play a role in improved performance.
